open_questions/1.rationale: The penetrance figure quoted to a family decides whether a genotype-positive relative is told they have a substantial chance of developing disease or a small one, so this discrepancy is not academic. Family cohorts give incomplete but substantial penetrance that roughly doubles after age 40, whereas unselected population cohorts give far lower estimates. The two populations differ in ascertainment - families are ascertained through an affected proband and are therefore enriched for whatever made that proband affected - but they may also differ in modifier burden, comorbidity and physical-activity exposure. Until those sources are separated, neither number is straightforwardly the right one to counsel with, which is why this entry records the family-cohort figures with their ascertainment context rather than presenting a single penetrance value.

evidence.snippet: Expectedly, knock-in of Mybpc3c.2373InsG resulted in the absence of cMyBP-C and our 18-28 week old homozygous Mybpc3c.2373InsG model developed cardiac hypertrophy and severe left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction, whereas HCM was not evident in Mybpc3+/InsG mice.
evidence.explanation: Documents the phenotype-negative heterozygote alongside the severely affected homozygote in the same allelic series.

evidence.snippet: We report a significant decrease in the proportion of myosin heads in the SRX state in homozygous cMyBP-C knockout mice, however heterozygous cMyBP-C knockout mice do not significantly differ from the wild type.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of the heterozygous-negative result at the molecular level, in a different mouse line with a different assay.

open_questions/2.rationale: This entry curates a mouse allelic series as experimental confirmation of the dose gradient, and for the homozygous pole that is exactly what it provides. The heterozygous pole is where model and disease part company: knock-in heterozygotes for the Dutch founder variant did not develop HCM at the ages studied, and the same negative result appears independently in the super-relaxed-state measurements, where heterozygous cMyBP-C knockout mice were indistinguishable from wild type while homozygotes showed a clear deficit. Human heterozygotes are the common form of this disease. The divergence is mechanistically informative rather than merely technical - it is consistent with the compensation capacity documented in heterozygous human iPSC cardiomyocytes, and it suggests murine heterozygotes may model the genotype-positive, phenotype-negative carrier rather than the patient. It also constrains what the models can be used for: a heterozygous mouse cannot demonstrate that a therapy prevents phenotype conversion if it never converts.

open_questions/3.rationale: Two features that define this disease clinically are absent from the models used to study it. Myocyte disarray is the pathognomonic human histological lesion and is documented in human MYBPC3 hearts; the mouse allelic series curated in this entry reports echocardiography, histology and cardiomyocyte contractility without reporting disarray, and engineered cardiac tissue has no ventricular architecture within which disarray could even be defined. Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction with systolic anterior motion - the target of both approved drugs and the endpoint of every trial cited here - depends on ventricular geometry and mitral-apparatus anatomy that small-animal and engineered-tissue systems do not reproduce. The practical consequence is a division of evidential labour that this entry makes explicit: the models carry the molecular and dose arguments, while every claim about relief of obstruction rests entirely on human trial data.

evidence.snippet: microdeletion of part of the SLC3A1 and PREPL genes on chromosome 2p21 was found.
evidence.explanation: The founding cohort directly identifies the contiguous SLC3A1/PREPL deletion.

evidence.snippet: Whole exome sequencing (WES), however, revealed a homozygous 2p21 deletion involving two contiquous genes, SLC3A1 (deletion of exons 2-10) and PREPL (deletion of exons 2-14).
evidence.explanation: This later sibling report confirms exon-level SLC3A1/PREPL deletion as the molecular diagnosis.

steps/2.description: Biallelic deletion of adjacent SLC3A1 and PREPL sequences on chromosome 2p21 is the upstream lesion that couples type A cystinuria with the neuromuscular, feeding, and growth phenotype.

evidence.snippet: SLC3A1 (chromosome 2p21) encodes the heavy subunit rBAT of a renal b(0,+) transporter
evidence.explanation: This supports the SLC3A1 transporter role in renal cystine handling.

evidence.snippet: Both genes are expressed in the renal proximal tubule and in the intestine and encode for different subunits of the transporter of dibasic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine)
evidence.explanation: This links the affected transporter system to proximal tubular and intestinal amino acid transport.

steps/3.description: Loss of the SLC3A1-encoded rBAT heavy subunit disrupts proximal tubular and intestinal cystine and dibasic amino acid transport, causing increased urinary cystine and cystine stone risk.

evidence.snippet: Such transporters deficiency leads to an accumulation of cystine in the urinary tract and to subsequent recurrent stones production, which can eventually lead to end stage renal disease.
evidence.explanation: This supports the causal step from transporter deficiency to cystine accumulation and recurrent stone formation.

steps/4.description: Increased urinary cystine concentration can exceed solubility, forming cystine crystals and stones that may obstruct the urinary tract.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of HCS can be difficult because neurological signs are aspecific and kidney stones are commonly absent during the first months of life.
evidence.explanation: This explains why renal stone disease may not be present early despite the underlying cystinuria.

steps/5.description: Cystine stones may occur later than the initial hypotonia presentation, so biochemical cystinuria can precede clinically apparent nephrolithiasis.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of HCS are type A cystinuria, growth hormone deficiency, muscle weakness, ptosis, and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: This connects PREPL deficiency with the neuromuscular and endocrine phenotype seen in HCS.

evidence.snippet: Isolated PREPL deficiency is a novel monogenic disorder that causes a congenital myasthenic syndrome with pre- and postsynaptic features and growth hormone deficiency.
evidence.explanation: This supports a neuromuscular-transmission mechanism for PREPL-related hypotonia and weakness.

steps/6.description: PREPL loss causes a congenital myasthenic syndrome with impaired neuromuscular transmission, explaining hypotonia, weakness, ptosis, and neonatal feeding problems in HCS and isolated PREPL deficiency.

evidence.snippet: PREPL deficiency causes neonatal hypotonia, ptosis, neonatal feeding difficulties, childhood obesity, xerostomia, and growth hormone deficiency.
evidence.explanation: The PREPL deficiency delineation paper directly supports the growth, obesity, feeding, xerostomia, and endocrine branch.

evidence.snippet: and failure to thrive, followed by hyperphagia and rapid weight gain in late childhood.
evidence.explanation: The founding HCS report supports the temporal pattern from early failure to thrive to later hyperphagia and rapid weight gain.

steps/7.description: PREPL deficiency contributes to growth hormone deficiency, neonatal feeding problems, early failure to thrive, and later appetite or weight-gain abnormalities including hyperphagia and childhood obesity.

evidence.snippet: Clinical features include cystinuria, neonatal hypotonia with spontaneous improvement, poor feeding in neonates, hyperphagia in childhood, growth hormone deficiency, and variable cognitive problems.
evidence.explanation: This supports variable cognitive involvement in HCS.

evidence.snippet: Patients present with generalized hypotonia at birth, nephrolithiasis, growth hormone deficiency, minor facial dysmorphism, and failure to thrive
evidence.explanation: The founding paper lists minor facial dysmorphism among presenting features.

steps/8.description: HCS has variable developmental, cognitive or neurobehavioral involvement, and minor dysmorphic features, but the intermediate mechanisms connecting the 2p21 deletion to these features remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Patients present with generalized hypotonia at birth, nephrolithiasis, growth hormone deficiency, minor facial dysmorphism, and failure to thrive
evidence.explanation: The founding cohort lists generalized hypotonia at birth as a presenting feature.

steps/9.description: Generalized neonatal or infantile hypotonia is a defining feature of HCS.

evidence.snippet: Clinical features include cystinuria, neonatal hypotonia with spontaneous improvement, poor feeding in neonates, hyperphagia in childhood, growth hormone deficiency, and variable cognitive problems.
evidence.explanation: This directly documents cystinuria as part of the HCS clinical feature set.

steps/10.description: Increased urinary cystine reflects the SLC3A1-mediated amino acid transport defect.

evidence.snippet: After 3 months, a percutaneous nephrolithotripsy was performed to treat the staghorn stone
evidence.explanation: This HCS case directly documents clinically significant cystine stone disease requiring intervention.

evidence.snippet: Later in childhood, the brother developed cystinuria and nephrolithiasis whereas the older sister suffered from cystinuria and chronic neurobehavioral disturbances.
evidence.explanation: This sibling report supports later childhood nephrolithiasis and variable expression.

steps/11.description: Cystine stones may develop from the cystinuria component and can cause obstructive urinary tract morbidity.

evidence.snippet: Two siblings presented similarly with congenital hypotonia, lactic acidosis, and failure to thrive.
evidence.explanation: This directly documents failure to thrive in HCS siblings.

steps/12.description: Poor early growth and feeding difficulty are common early manifestations.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of HCS are type A cystinuria, growth hormone deficiency, muscle weakness, ptosis, and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: This directly identifies growth hormone deficiency as a major HCS feature.

steps/13.description: Growth hormone deficiency contributes to the short-stature and growth-failure component of HCS.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of HCS are type A cystinuria, growth hormone deficiency, muscle weakness, ptosis, and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: This directly lists muscle weakness as a major clinical feature of HCS.

steps/14.description: Muscle weakness is part of the PREPL-related neuromuscular phenotype and is distinct from neonatal hypotonia.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of HCS are type A cystinuria, growth hormone deficiency, muscle weakness, ptosis, and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: This directly lists ptosis as a major clinical feature of HCS.

steps/15.description: Ptosis is a major PREPL-related neuromuscular feature in HCS and isolated PREPL deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Clinical features include cystinuria, neonatal hypotonia with spontaneous improvement, poor feeding in neonates, hyperphagia in childhood, growth hormone deficiency, and variable cognitive problems.
evidence.explanation: This directly documents childhood hyperphagia in the HCS clinical feature list.

evidence.snippet: and failure to thrive, followed by hyperphagia and rapid weight gain in late childhood.
evidence.explanation: This supports the temporal pattern of early failure to thrive followed by late-childhood hyperphagia and weight gain.

steps/16.description: Hyperphagia can emerge in childhood after early failure to thrive and poor feeding.

evidence.snippet: PREPL deficiency causes neonatal hypotonia, ptosis, neonatal feeding difficulties, childhood obesity, xerostomia, and growth hormone deficiency.
evidence.explanation: The PREPL deficiency delineation paper explicitly lists childhood obesity among PREPL-associated phenotypes, including HCS subjects.

steps/17.description: Childhood obesity can emerge after the early failure-to-thrive phase and is a named PREPL deficiency feature.

evidence.snippet: patients homozygous for these deletions suffer from a general neonatal hypotonia and growth retardation in addition to cystinuria.
evidence.explanation: Growth retardation is a documented feature of HCS.

evidence.snippet: HP:0002644 | Abnormality of pelvic girdle bone morphology | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists abnormality of pelvic girdle bone morphology as a very frequent feature of Jeune syndrome.

evidence.snippet: characterized by short ribs and a narrow thorax, short long bones, inconstant polydactyly, and trident acetabular roof.
evidence.explanation: The trident acetabular roof is a pathognomonic pelvic skeletal feature of JATD used for diagnosis.

steps/14.description: Abnormality of pelvic girdle bone morphology, including the trident acetabular roof (acetabular spurs), is a very frequent and pathognomonic radiographic finding in Jeune syndrome.

evidence.snippet: HP:0002652 | Skeletal dysplasia | Very frequent (99-80%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists skeletal dysplasia as a very frequent feature of Jeune syndrome.

steps/15.description: Generalized skeletal dysplasia is the overarching phenotype of JATD, encompassing the short ribs, limb shortening, and pelvic/metaphyseal changes due to ciliary IFT dysfunction affecting chondrocyte signaling.

evidence.snippet: HP:0010579 | Cone-shaped epiphysis | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists cone-shaped epiphysis as a frequent feature of Jeune syndrome.

steps/16.description: Cone-shaped epiphyses, particularly of the phalanges, are a frequent radiographic finding in JATD, arising from the Hedgehog signaling defect in chondrocytes at the growth plates.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001156 | Brachydactyly | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists brachydactyly as a frequent feature of Jeune syndrome.

steps/17.description: Shortening of the digits (brachydactyly) is a frequent skeletal feature of JATD, reflecting the generalized chondrodysplasia affecting phalangeal growth.

evidence.snippet: HP:0000944 | Abnormal metaphysis morphology | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists abnormal metaphysis morphology as a frequent feature of Jeune syndrome.

steps/18.description: Metaphyseal changes (irregular, widened or spurred metaphyses) are a frequent radiographic feature of JATD, reflecting the impaired endochondral ossification in ciliopathy-driven chondrodysplasia.

evidence.snippet: HP:0000889 | Abnormality of the clavicle | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet lists abnormality of the clavicle as a frequent feature of Jeune syndrome.

steps/19.description: Clavicular abnormalities are a frequent skeletal finding in JATD, part of the generalized ciliopathy-related chondrodysplasia affecting the thoracic skeleton.

evidence.snippet: identified homozygous mutations in the cytoplasmic dynein 2 heavy chain 1 (DYNC2H1) gene in the affected children.
evidence.explanation: Identifies DYNC2H1 as a causative gene for JATD.

evidence.snippet: We detected 34 DYNC2H1 mutations in 29/71 (41%) patients from 19/57 families (33%), showing it as a major cause of JATD especially in Northern European patients.
evidence.explanation: Large cohort showing DYNC2H1 mutations in 41% of JATD patients, establishing it as the most common genetic cause.

evidence.snippet: DYNC2H1 patients largely lacked significant extra-skeletal involvement, demonstrating an important genotype-phenotype correlation in JATD.
evidence.explanation: Important genotype-phenotype correlation showing DYNC2H1 patients have primarily skeletal disease.

evidence.snippet: We identified DYNC2H1 mutations in 23 families (59%) and IFT80 mutations in two families (5%).
evidence.explanation: French cohort showing DYNC2H1 mutations in 59% of JATD families.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic mutations in DYNC2H1, encoding the heavy chain of cytoplasmic dynein-2. The most common genetic cause of JATD, accounting for 33-59% of families depending on the cohort. DYNC2H1 patients tend to have a primarily skeletal phenotype without major extra-skeletal involvement.

evidence.snippet: We show that IFT80 mutations underlie a subset of Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy cases, establishing the first association of a defective intraflagellar transport (IFT) protein with human disease.
evidence.explanation: First identification of IFT80 as a causative gene for JATD.

evidence.snippet: We identified DYNC2H1 mutations in 23 families (59%) and IFT80 mutations in two families (5%).
evidence.explanation: Confirms IFT80 is a rare cause of JATD at 5% of families.

genes/1.notes: Biallelic mutations in IFT80, encoding intraflagellar transport protein 80. IFT80 is a component of the IFT-B complex required for anterograde transport in cilia. A rare cause of JATD (5%).

genes/2.notes: Biallelic mutations in IFT140, encoding a component of the IFT-A complex involved in retrograde intraflagellar transport.

evidence.snippet: Our findings expand the mutation spectrum of DYNC2H1, IFT172 and WDR19 associated with skeletal ciliopathies, and provide useful information for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling on rare skeletal disorders.
evidence.explanation: Prenatal case series confirms WDR19 as causative in skeletal ciliopathy spectrum including JATD.

genes/3.notes: Biallelic mutations in WDR19, encoding another IFT-A complex component. WDR19 mutations also cause cranioectodermal dysplasia and nephronophthisis.

evidence.snippet: WDR34 mutations led to different spectrums of phenotypes. Quantitative proteomics demonstrated changes in dynein-2 assembly, whereas initiation and extension of the axoneme, localization of intraflagellar transport complex-B proteins, transition zone integrity and Hedgehog signalling were also affected.
evidence.explanation: Published in vitro characterization of WDR34 JATD mutations demonstrates diverse molecular consequences in dynein-2 assembly, IFT-B localization, transition zone integrity, and Hedgehog signaling, establishing WDR34 as causative and mechanistically complex.

genes/4.notes: Biallelic mutations in WDR34 (DYNC2I2), encoding dynein-2 intermediate chain 3. Disease-associated WDR34 mutations produce a diverse spectrum of molecular defects including dynein-2 assembly disruption, IFT-B protein mislocalization, transition zone integrity loss, and Hedgehog signaling impairment. This mechanistic heterogeneity underlies the variable expressivity of WDR34-associated JATD.

evidence.snippet: Our findings expand the mutation spectrum of DYNC2H1, IFT172 and WDR19 associated with skeletal ciliopathies, and provide useful information for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling on rare skeletal disorders.
evidence.explanation: Prenatal case series confirms IFT172 as causative in skeletal ciliopathy spectrum including JATD/SRTD10.

genes/5.notes: Biallelic mutations in IFT172, encoding a structural component of the IFT-B complex required for anterograde ciliary transport. IFT172 mutations cause skeletal ciliopathy recognized prenatally by narrow thorax and short long bones. Corresponds to SRTD10.

evidence.snippet: Homozygous exon 2 deletion cases presented a ciliary chondrodysplasia with narrow thorax and progressive growth retardation along with a mucociliary clearance disorder phenotype with severely shorted cilia.
evidence.explanation: Reports IFT74 exon 2 deletion causing ciliary chondrodysplasia with narrow thorax and mucociliary clearance disorder, confirming IFT74 as causative in JATD spectrum with a distinctive motile cilia crossover phenotype.

genes/6.notes: Biallelic mutations in IFT74, encoding the tubulin-binding subunit of the IFT-B complex. Exhibits allele-specific phenotypes: exon 2 deletion alleles produce ciliary chondrodysplasia with narrow thorax plus mucociliary clearance disorder (combined primary and motile cilia phenotype), while splice site variants cause lethal skeletal chondrodysplasia. This dual primary/motile cilia involvement is mechanistically explained by the higher demand for tubulin transport in motile cilia.

evidence.snippet: impaired function of GRK2 compromises cilia-based signaling of Hedgehog pathway as well as Wnt signaling, while cilia morphology remains intact
evidence.explanation: Establishes GRK2 as a novel JATD mechanism via Hedgehog/Wnt signaling impairment independent of structural IFT defects or cilia morphology changes.

genes/7.notes: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in GRK2 produce a Jeune syndrome phenotype via impairment of cilia-based Hedgehog and Wnt signaling without structural cilia abnormalities. This non-IFT mechanism identifies GRK2 as a regulator of ciliary Smoothened phosphorylation required for skeletogenesis. Evidence is currently limited to a single case report (2024); replication in additional families is needed.

treatments/0.description: Mechanical ventilation and respiratory support in neonates with severe thoracic restriction. May require prolonged ventilatory support or tracheostomy.

evidence.snippet: Survival rate of the 22 patients was 68%.
evidence.explanation: Reports 68% survival rate with VEPTR surgical treatment.

evidence.snippet: The survival rate in JS with surgery was nearly 70% (compared with 70% to 80% mortality without treatment) with less ventilator dependence.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates dramatic improvement in survival with VEPTR surgery compared to untreated JATD.

evidence.snippet: Average chest width increased from 121 to 168 mm at follow-up (P<0.001).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the significant increase in thoracic dimensions achieved by VEPTR expansion surgery.

treatments/1.description: Vertical expandable prosthetic titanium rib (VEPTR) to increase thoracic volume and improve respiratory function. Surgery achieves nearly 70% survival compared to 70-80% mortality without treatment.

treatments/2.description: Monitoring and management of progressive renal cystic disease, including dialysis or transplantation for end-stage renal failure.

evidence.snippet: Renal and liver diseases occurred respectively in 17% and 22% of cases
evidence.explanation: Quantifies hepatic involvement at 22% of postnatal JATD cases, establishing the need for routine hepatology surveillance.

treatments/3.description: Monitoring for hepatic fibrosis and biliary dysgenesis, which occurs in 22% of postnatal JATD cases. Includes serial liver function testing and hepatic ultrasound with hepatology referral. Liver disease may progress to biliary cirrhosis in a subset of patients requiring hepatological management.

evidence.snippet: retinal alteration was present in 50% of cases aged more than 5 years.
evidence.explanation: Documents high frequency of retinal dystrophy in JATD patients over age 5, justifying routine ophthalmologic surveillance starting in early childhood.

treatments/4.description: Regular ophthalmologic evaluation for retinal dystrophy, which occurs in 50% of JATD patients over age 5. Surveillance should begin in early childhood. Low-vision aids for affected patients; no disease-modifying therapy currently exists for the retinal disease component.

treatments/5.description: Genetic counseling for families regarding the 25% recurrence risk with autosomal recessive inheritance, prenatal diagnosis options (fetal exome sequencing of JATD genes), carrier testing for family members, and distinguishing JATD from lethal short-rib polydactyly syndromes in the prenatal setting.

evidence.snippet: KCNB1 encodes the alpha subunit of the KV2.1 voltage-gated potassium channel, a delayed rectifier potassium channel that is an important regulator of neuronal excitability.
evidence.explanation: Identifies KCNB1/Kv2.1 as the delayed-rectifier channel whose de novo variants trigger the disorder.

evidence.snippet: The voltage-gated Kv2.1 potassium channel encoded by KCNB1 produces the major delayed rectifier potassium current in pyramidal neurons.
evidence.explanation: Establishes Kv2.1 as the major delayed-rectifier current of pyramidal neurons, the channel altered by the variant.

steps/1.description: De novo heterozygous KCNB1 variants, most located in the pore/selectivity-filter and voltage-sensor regions of the channel, alter the function of Kv2.1, the alpha subunit of the delayed-rectifier voltage-gated potassium channel that is the major delayed-rectifier K+ current of cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons and an important regulator of neuronal excitability. This is the upstream molecular trigger of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: the mutation in the channel pore domain (p.G401R) selectively abolished endogenous Kv2 currents in transfected pyramidal neurons, indicating a dominant-negative effect.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the dominant-negative suppression of the Kv2 delayed-rectifier current by a pore-domain variant.

evidence.snippet: All three mutants exhibited loss of K+ selectivity
evidence.explanation: Shows loss of potassium selectivity for selectivity-filter/pore variants, the basis for an aberrant depolarizing cation conductance.

evidence.snippet: These gain-of-function and dominant-negative functional defects are predicted to result in depolarized resting membrane potential and impaired membrane repolarization, with increased cellular excitability as a net consequence.
evidence.explanation: Links the dominant-negative and gain-of-function defects to impaired repolarization and increased excitability.

evidence.snippet: These voltage-activated Kv2.1 V378A currents were nonselective among monovalent cations.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that a disease variant abolishes K+ selectivity, producing a nonselective cation current.

steps/2.description: Mutant Kv2.1 subunits co-assemble with wild-type subunits into heterotetrameric channels, so a single variant allele suppresses the delayed-rectifier K+ current in a dominant-negative fashion. Pore-domain variants can selectively abolish the endogenous Kv2 current, while selectivity-filter variants additionally cause loss of K+ selectivity, rendering the channel a nonselective, depolarizing cation conductance. Loss of the repolarizing delayed-rectifier current, together with an aberrant inward cation current, is predicted to depolarize the resting membrane potential and impair membrane repolarization.

evidence.snippet: Kv2.1 localizes to dense, cell-surface clusters that contain non-conducting channels, indicating that they have a function that is unrelated to membrane-potential regulation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the non-conducting clustered pool of Kv2.1 with a function independent of current conduction.

evidence.snippet: the clustered Kv2.1 plays a direct structural role in the induction of stable ER-plasma-membrane junctions in both transfected HEK 293 cells and cultured hippocampal neurons.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the direct structural role of clustered Kv2.1 in organizing ER-plasma-membrane junctions.

evidence.snippet: we suggest that defects in expression and subcellular localization of Kv2.1 V378A channels could contribute to the pathophysiology of this KCNB1 variant.
evidence.explanation: Links disease-variant defects in Kv2.1 expression and localization directly to the pathophysiology.

steps/3.description: Beyond conducting current, Kv2.1 localizes to dense surface clusters of largely non-conducting channels that play a direct structural role in forming stable endoplasmic reticulum-plasma-membrane junctions, which serve as membrane-trafficking and Ca2+-signaling hubs. Disease variants perturb Kv2.1 expression and subcellular localization and reciprocally alter the trafficking of co-assembled wild-type subunits, so this non-conducting scaffolding role is an independent, conductance-separable arm of the pathophysiology.

evidence.snippet: These gain-of-function and dominant-negative functional defects are predicted to result in depolarized resting membrane potential and impaired membrane repolarization, with increased cellular excitability as a net consequence.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports increased neuronal excitability as the net functional consequence of the channel defect, shifting the excitation-inhibition balance.

steps/4.description: Loss of the repolarizing delayed-rectifier current and an aberrant depolarizing cation conductance disturb the excitability of cortical and hippocampal neurons. In heterologous studies the dominant-negative and gain-of-function defects predict depolarized resting potential and increased cellular excitability, whereas neuronal studies of some variants show impaired repetitive firing of pyramidal cells; both routes converge on a disturbed balance between excitatory and inhibitory signaling in cortical networks.

evidence.snippet: novel de novo heterozygous missense KCNB1 mutations in two patients showing psychomotor developmental delay and severe infantile generalized seizures with high-amplitude spike-and-wave electroencephalogram discharges.
evidence.explanation: Documents the electroclinical seizure phenotype produced by the hypersynchronous network excitability disturbance.

steps/5.description: The net excitatory bias produces a hyperexcitable, hypersynchronous cortical and hippocampal network state that converts the altered excitability into paroxysmal discharges, manifesting clinically as infantile-onset seizures with high-amplitude spike-and-wave electroencephalographic discharges.

evidence.snippet: insufficient firing of pyramidal neurons would disturb both development and stability of neuronal circuits, leading to the disease phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Links the neuronal firing defect to disturbed circuit development, the basis of the neurodevelopmental phenotype.

evidence.snippet: showed developmental delay in all with severe to profound intellectual disability in 67% (n = 41/61) and autistic features in 56%
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the near-universal developmental delay and severe-to-profound intellectual disability that define the neurodevelopmental outcome.

steps/6.description: Abnormal excitability and disturbed activity-dependent signaling during a critical developmental window impair maturation and stability of cortical neuronal circuits. Insufficient or dysregulated pyramidal-neuron firing is predicted to disturb both the development and the stability of neuronal networks, producing developmental delay in essentially all patients, with frequently severe-to-profound intellectual disability, autistic features, and behavioral problems that are partly independent of seizure burden.

evidence.snippet: Twenty patients (56%) had DEE with infantile onset seizures
evidence.explanation: Documents developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with infantile-onset seizures as the predominant presentation.

steps/7.description: A large proportion of patients have a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with infantile-onset seizures; others fall along a spectrum to developmental encephalopathy with later-onset or no epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: 9 patients (36%) starting with epileptic spasms between 3 and 18 months of age.
evidence.explanation: Documents epileptic spasms as an infantile-onset seizure type in a defined fraction of patients.

steps/8.description: A substantial subset of patients present with epileptic spasms in infancy, typically between 3 and 18 months of age.

evidence.snippet: All patients had developmental delay, with 17 (65%) experiencing severe developmental delay
evidence.explanation: Establishes developmental delay as a universal feature, severe in most.

steps/9.description: Developmental delay is essentially universal, spanning motor, language, and cognitive domains.

evidence.snippet: severe to profound intellectual disability in 67% (n = 41/61)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies severe-to-profound intellectual disability across the pooled cohort.

steps/10.description: Intellectual disability is frequently severe to profound, and is more marked in individuals with the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy end of the spectrum.

evidence.snippet: autistic features in 56% (n = 32/57).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies autistic features as a frequent neurodevelopmental comorbidity.

steps/11.description: Autistic features are common in KCNB1-related encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: 20 (77%) carried a missense variant in the ion channel domain of KCNB1, with a concentration of variants in region S5 to S6.
evidence.explanation: Documents the concentration of pathogenic missense variants in the pore-forming ion-channel domain.

evidence.snippet: Missense variants were associated with more frequent and more severe epilepsy compared to truncating variants.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the genotype-phenotype correlation between variant class and epilepsy severity.

genes/0.notes: De novo heterozygous KCNB1 variants cause the disorder. Missense variants concentrate in the ion-channel domain, particularly the S5-S6 pore/selectivity filter and the voltage-sensor region, and are associated with more frequent and more severe epilepsy; truncating variants tend to produce a milder phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Rare GTCS are controlled with levetiracetam and clonazepam, but other seizure types have been poorly controlled with multiple therapies that were ineffective or limited by side effects
evidence.explanation: Documents levetiracetam use with partial seizure control and frequent treatment resistance in a KCNB1 patient.

treatments/0.description: Seizures are managed with antiseizure medications, but epilepsy is frequently treatment-resistant and no agent corrects the underlying Kv2.1 channel defect. Agents such as levetiracetam are used, with variable and often incomplete response.

evidence.snippet: Rare GTCS are controlled with levetiracetam and clonazepam, but other seizure types have been poorly controlled with multiple therapies that were ineffective or limited by side effects
evidence.explanation: Levetiracetam partially controls some seizure types, consistent with symptomatic suppression of the hyperexcitable network state, but does not address the underlying channel defect.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Antiseizure medications such as levetiracetam act symptomatically to dampen the hyperexcitable, hypersynchronous network discharges rather than correcting the upstream Kv2.1 channel defect, giving variable and often incomplete seizure control.

evidence.snippet: Further understanding of disease mechanisms should facilitate the development of targeted therapies, much needed to improve the neurodevelopmental prognosis.
evidence.explanation: Highlights the current absence of targeted therapy and reliance on supportive management.

treatments/1.description: Multidisciplinary developmental therapies and supportive care are the mainstay given the severe neurodevelopmental impairment; targeted disease-modifying therapies are not yet available and are much needed.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling addresses the de novo dominant mechanism and the generally low recurrence risk, with attention to the rare possibility of parental mosaicism.

evidence.snippet: These gain-of-function and dominant-negative functional defects are predicted to result in depolarized resting membrane potential and impaired membrane repolarization, with increased cellular excitability as a net consequence.
evidence.explanation: Supports the net-hyperexcitability account arising from selectivity-filter/pore variants.

evidence.snippet: Both mutants inhibited repetitive neuronal firing through preventing production of deep interspike voltages.
evidence.explanation: Supports the competing reduced-firing account, in which impaired repetitive firing destabilizes circuits.

evidence.snippet: Reduction of delayed rectifier potassium current by Kcnb1 deletion in mice results in reduced thresholds to induced seizures, but not spontaneous seizures.
evidence.explanation: The Kcnb1-deletion mouse is the explicit loss-of-function counterweight to the human gain-of-function/dominant-negative result: pure loss of Kv2.1 current lowers induced-seizure threshold but does not reproduce spontaneous epileptic encephalopathy, sharpening the open question of which mechanism drives the human disease.

open_questions/0.rationale: Heterologous expression of pore/selectivity-filter variants shows loss of K+ selectivity plus dominant-negative and gain-of-function defects predicted to depolarize neurons and increase excitability. In contrast, neuronal studies of other variants report that mutants inhibit repetitive firing of pyramidal neurons, so that insufficient firing disturbs circuit development and stability. These are mechanistically opposite accounts of how the same channel defect produces epilepsy and encephalopathy, and reconciling them, potentially by variant class or by excitatory-versus-inhibitory cell-type effects, is prerequisite to rational, mechanism-matched therapy.

evidence.snippet: Kv2.1 localizes to dense, cell-surface clusters that contain non-conducting channels, indicating that they have a function that is unrelated to membrane-potential regulation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the conductance-independent structural role whose disease contribution is the open question.

evidence.snippet: Striking cell background-dependent differences in expression and subcellular localization of the V378A mutation were observed in heterologous cells.
evidence.explanation: Shows a disease variant disrupts Kv2.1 localization, the scaffolding arm whose phenotypic weight is unresolved.

open_questions/1.rationale: Kv2.1 has a well-established conductance-independent role in forming ER-plasma-membrane junctions that serve as membrane-trafficking and Ca2+-signaling hubs, and disease variants alter Kv2.1 expression and subcellular localization. It is not yet resolved whether the encephalopathy phenotype depends on this scaffolding defect in addition to the conduction defect, which matters for whether therapies must restore channel gating, channel localization/clustering, or both.

evidence.snippet: about 20% of cases of LKS, CSWSS and electroclinically atypical rolandic epilepsy often associated with speech impairment can have a genetic origin sustained by de novo or inherited mutations in the GRIN2A gene (encoding the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor α2 subunit, GluN2A)
evidence.explanation: Establishes GRIN2A/NMDA receptor (GluN2A) dysfunction as the molecular basis in a substantial subset of LKS.

evidence.snippet: We report the first monogenic cause, to our knowledge, for EAS. GRIN2A mutations are restricted to this group of cases
evidence.explanation: Identifies GRIN2A as the first monogenic cause of epilepsy-aphasia syndromes, of which LKS is the prototype.

steps/1.description: In approximately 20% of LKS/epilepsy-aphasia spectrum cases, de novo or inherited pathogenic variants in GRIN2A alter the function of the GluN2A (NR2A) subunit of the NMDA glutamate receptor. Disrupted NMDA receptor signaling perturbs excitatory glutamatergic neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity in cortical neurons, providing the molecular substrate for the epileptic encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: It is thought to be the result of an epileptogenic lesion arising in speech cortex during a critical period of development.
evidence.explanation: Supports the model that an epileptogenic focus in speech cortex during a developmental critical period drives the language disorder.

evidence.snippet: RE is part of a single and continuous spectrum of childhood epilepsies and epileptic encephalopathies with acquired cognitive, behavioral and speech and/or language impairment, known as the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum (EAS)
evidence.explanation: Frames LKS within the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum in which sleep-activated epileptiform activity produces acquired language and cognitive impairment.

steps/2.description: Pathological hyperexcitability produces marked activation of focal, typically perisylvian/centrotemporal, spike-and-wave discharges during non-REM (slow-wave) sleep, reaching continuous or near-continuous spike and waves during slow sleep (electrical status epilepticus in sleep, ESES/CSWS). This sleep-potentiated epileptiform activity in language cortex is thought to disrupt the maturation and function of language networks during a critical developmental window.

evidence.snippet: Anomalies in perisylvian regions, with largest differences in Broca's area, suggest an altered development of classical speech-language networks in GRIN2A-related EAS.
evidence.explanation: Structural MRI in GRIN2A-variant individuals demonstrates perisylvian and hippocampal anomalies consistent with disrupted speech-language network development.

steps/3.description: Structural MRI in individuals with pathogenic GRIN2A variants and epilepsy-aphasia syndromes shows altered development of classical speech-language networks: increased cortical thickness/volume in perisylvian regions (posterior Broca's area, superior temporal region) and reduced left hippocampal volume, indicating that NMDA-receptor dysfunction perturbs speech-language network development.

evidence.snippet: Epilepsy-aphasia syndromes (EAS) are a group of rare, severe epileptic encephalopathies of unknown etiology with a characteristic electroencephalogram (EEG) pattern and developmental regression particularly affecting language.
evidence.explanation: Supports the core LKS phenotype of developmental regression preferentially affecting language.

steps/4.description: Sleep-activated epileptiform disruption of perisylvian language cortex produces acquired loss of previously developed language, characteristically beginning with impaired auditory verbal comprehension (auditory verbal agnosia) and progressing to broader receptive and expressive language loss, sometimes with associated behavioral and cognitive regression.

evidence.snippet: Patients with pathogenic variants in GRIN2A offer an opportunity to interrogate the impact of glutamate receptor dysfunction on brain development.
evidence.explanation: Links GRIN2A glutamate-receptor dysfunction to altered speech-language network brain development.

edges/1.description: NMDA-receptor (GluN2A) dysfunction perturbs development of perisylvian speech-language networks and the hippocampus.

evidence.snippet: voltage-independent glutamate-gated signaling of GluN2A-containing NMDA receptors is associated with NMDAR-dependent audiogenic seizures due to hyperexcitable midbrain circuits
evidence.explanation: A Grin2a gene-targeted mouse model demonstrates that altered GluN2A NMDA receptor signaling produces a hyperexcitable, seizure-prone substrate, supporting the link from GRIN2A dysfunction to epileptiform activity.

edges/2.description: Altered NMDA-receptor (GluN2A) signaling produces a hyperexcitable cortical/subcortical substrate that gives rise to sleep-activated epileptiform activity.

evidence.snippet: Landau-Kleffner syndrome (LKS) is an acquired epileptic aphasia occurring in childhood and associated with a generally poor prognosis for recovery of speech.
evidence.explanation: Characterizes LKS as an acquired epileptic aphasia, supporting the causal link from the epileptogenic activity in speech cortex to the acquired language regression.

edges/3.description: Sleep-activated epileptiform activity in speech cortex drives the acquired language regression.

evidence.snippet: about 20% of cases of LKS, CSWSS and electroclinically atypical rolandic epilepsy often associated with speech impairment can have a genetic origin sustained by de novo or inherited mutations in the GRIN2A gene
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the GRIN2A contribution (~20%) to LKS and related EAS disorders.

evidence.snippet: all four families presented with EAS, accounting for 9% of epilepsy-aphasia cases
evidence.explanation: Independent cohort confirming GRIN2A variants segregating in epilepsy-aphasia spectrum families.

genes/0.notes: GRIN2A encodes the GluN2A subunit of the NMDA glutamate receptor. Variants include null/loss-of-function, missense (loss- or gain-of-function), and deletions; functional class has therapeutic implications.

evidence.snippet: Steroid treatment was most successful in improving cognitive performance.
evidence.explanation: A retrospective cohort of children with electrical status epilepticus in sleep (the electrographic substrate of LKS) found steroid treatment most successful in improving cognition, supporting corticosteroid use.

evidence.snippet: In (D)EE-SWAS (nine studies, 126 patients), 64% of patients showed an improvement either in the EEG or in their language/cognition following various steroid treatment regimes.
evidence.explanation: A systematic review quantifies corticosteroid response in DEE-SWAS (which includes LKS), with 64% showing EEG or language/cognitive improvement.

treatments/0.description: Corticosteroids (and ACTH) are widely used to suppress the sleep-activated epileptiform activity and promote language recovery in LKS, particularly when started early.

evidence.snippet: In (D)EE-SWAS (nine studies, 126 patients), 64% of patients showed an improvement either in the EEG or in their language/cognition following various steroid treatment regimes.
evidence.explanation: Documents corticosteroid-driven EEG (epileptiform activity) improvement in DEE-SWAS including LKS, supporting that steroids act on the sleep-activated epileptiform mechanism.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Corticosteroids suppress the sleep-activated epileptiform activity (ESES), reducing the spike-wave index that drives cognitive/language decline.

evidence.snippet: There was no evidence from trials to support or refute the use of pharmacological treatment for continuous spike-wave during slow wave sleep syndrome or Landau-Kleffner syndrome.
evidence.explanation: A Cochrane systematic review documents the absence of randomized trial evidence for pharmacotherapy in LKS/CSWS, contextualizing the empirical basis of antiseizure drug use.

treatments/1.description: Anti-seizure medications are used to control clinical seizures; some conventional agents may worsen ESES, so agent selection is important. Note: a 2020 Cochrane review found no randomized trial evidence to support or refute pharmacological treatment for CSWS/LKS.

evidence.snippet: Benzodiazepines and ASMs are the most frequent initial therapy prescribed for CSWS in the US. Our data suggests that ASMs are inferior to benzodiazepines and steroids and support earlier use of these therapies.
evidence.explanation: A multicenter collaboration documents benzodiazepines as a common first-line CSWS/LKS therapy with outcomes superior to other antiseizure medications.

treatments/2.description: High-dose benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam, clobazam) are among the most frequently used first-line therapies for the sleep-activated epileptiform activity (ESES/CSWS) underlying LKS and the epilepsy-aphasia spectrum. In a multicenter cohort, benzodiazepines were associated with greater odds of clinical improvement than other antiseizure medications.

evidence.snippet: children had a greater odds of clinical improvement with benzodiazepines (OR 3.32, 95%CI 1.57-7.04, P = .002) or steroids (OR 4.04, 95%CI 1.41-11.59, P = .01) than with ASMs
evidence.explanation: A multicenter retrospective CSWS cohort found benzodiazepines superior to other antiseizure medications for clinical improvement, supporting their use against the sleep-activated epileptiform mechanism.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Benzodiazepines suppress the sleep-activated epileptiform activity (ESES/CSWS) that drives the cognitive and language decline.

evidence.snippet: treatment with the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) coagonist L-serine was associated with improvements in behavior, development, EEG features, and/or seizure frequency

steps/1.description: Homozygous or compound heterozygous KARS1 variants, mostly missense with occasional splice-site and frameshift alleles. evidence.snippet: Moreover, similarly disrupted lysyl-tRNA synthetase (LysRS) proteins showed reduced enzymatic activities and abnormal CNSs in Xenopus embryos.
evidence.explanation: Independent demonstration of reduced enzymatic activity for the disrupted protein, alongside a CNS phenotype in a model organism.

steps/2.description: Lysyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNA-Lys with lysine, the committed step that makes lysine available to the ribosome. Mutant enzymes show reduced aminoacylation activity in vitro, and the same reduction is seen in yeast complementation assays.

evidence.snippet: Molecular characterization of patient fibroblasts revealed a multiple oxidative phosphorylation deficiency due to impaired mitochondrial translation, but no evidence of inhibition of cytosolic translation.
evidence.explanation: Localises the translation defect to the mitochondrial compartment in patient cells, which is what this node claims.

evidence.snippet: Reintroduction of wild-type mitochondrial KARS, but not the cytosolic isoform, rescued this phenotype confirming the disease-causing nature of p.(Pro228Leu) exchange and demonstrating the mitochondrial etiology of the disease.
evidence.explanation: Isoform-specific rescue - the experiment that makes the mitochondrial arm a demonstrated mechanism rather than an inference from dual localisation.

steps/3.description: KARS1 produces both the cytosolic and the mitochondrial enzyme, and in the patient in whom the two compartments were separated experimentally, only the mitochondrial one was affected: patient fibroblasts had a multiple oxidative phosphorylation deficiency from impaired mitochondrial translation, with no cytosolic translation defect, and only the mitochondrial isoform rescued it.

evidence.snippet: We propose that mitochondrial translation deficiency is the probable disease culprit in this and possibly other patients with mutations in KARS.
evidence.explanation: States the authors' mechanistic conclusion linking the translation defect to the disease, which is the step this node sits on.

steps/4.description: Failure of mitochondrial translation leaves the respiratory chain short of its mitochondrially encoded subunits, giving a combined complex deficiency and a shift toward anaerobic metabolism. Clinically this surfaces as elevated lactate and pyruvate. The tissues that fail first are the ones with the highest oxidative demand, which is the conventional explanation for why a translation defect of this kind presents with cochlear and central nervous system disease; no source cited here demonstrates that ordering for KARS1 specifically.

steps/1.description: LIPT1 encodes lipoyltransferase 1, which transfers lipoyl groups from lipoyl-GCSH to the E2 subunits of pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. This is the final step in the mitochondrial lipoylation pathway. Crucially, LIPT1 is not required for lipoylation of GCSH itself, so the glycine cleavage system remains functional. This explains the distinctive biochemical signature: combined dehydrogenase deficiency with lactic acidosis but preserved glycine cleavage and normal glycine levels. The clinical consequence is a Leigh-like encephalopathy driven by energy failure rather than the combined energy failure plus glycine toxicity seen in LIPT2 and LIAS deficiency.

evidence.snippet: the absence of glycine elevation, the normal activity of the glycine cleavage system and the normal lipoylation of the H protein suggested a defect of lipoic acid transfer to particular proteins rather than a general impairment of lipoic acid biosynthesis
evidence.explanation: Key biochemical finding distinguishing LIPT1 from LIAS/LIPT2 deficiency: glycine cleavage is preserved because GCSH lipoylation is intact.

evidence.snippet: Patients that display absent or low lipoylation of all three enzymes have mutations in either of two genes LIAS or LIPT2 whereas patients that retain glycine cleavage activity are mutant in a third gene, LIPT1
evidence.explanation: Review explains the biochemical basis for classification of lipoylation disorders by glycine cleavage status.

evidence.snippet: LIPT1 patients generally suffer only the respiratory and muscle weakness problems because GCSH is lipoylated and glycine is cleaved
evidence.explanation: Confirms that LIPT1 patients retain GCSH lipoylation and therefore glycine cleavage activity, sparing them from glycine accumulation.

steps/2.description: Loss of LIPT1 function impairs lipoylation of the E2 subunits of PDHc, alpha-KGDHc, and BCKDHc, causing combined dehydrogenase deficiency with lactic acidosis and elevation of alpha-ketoacids. However, the glycine cleavage system H protein (GCSH) is lipoylated upstream by the LIPT2-LIAS pathway and does not require LIPT1 for its own lipoylation, so glycine cleavage is preserved and glycine levels remain normal or near-normal.

steps/3.description: LIPT1-deficient patient-derived fibroblasts show reduced PDH and alpha-KGDH activities with cellular bioenergetic failure, iron accumulation, and lipid peroxidation. evidence.snippet: Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive facultative intracellular pathogen that can cause severe invasive infections upon ingestion with contaminated food.
evidence.explanation: States that invasive infection follows ingestion of contaminated food, which is the exposure this entry records.

evidence.snippet: One key group of virulence factors are internalins (Inl, with InlA and InlB being the most known), which are surface proteins that mediate bacterial adherence and the invasion of host cells. These proteins interact with specific host–cell receptors, allowing LM to penetrate the intestinal epithelium and breach critical barriers such as the placental and blood–brain barriers.
evidence.explanation: Names the internalins, their receptor-mediated invasion, and the barriers they breach.

steps/1.description: InlA and InlB are surface proteins with leucine-rich repeats that bind host receptors and drive the bacterium into a cell that is not a phagocyte. InlA binds E-cadherin. The same family of proteins later carries the organism across the placental and blood-brain barriers, which is why one mechanism explains three tissue tropisms.

evidence.snippet: Another pivotal virulence factor is listeriolysin O (LLO), a pore-forming toxin that facilitates the bacterium’s escape from the phagosome into the host–cell’s cytoplasm following engulfment. This cholesterol-dependent cytolysin disrupts the phagosomal membrane, enabling LM to evade lysosomal degradation by the host immune system and establish a replicative niche within the cytoplasm
evidence.explanation: Describes the toxin, the membrane it disrupts and the escape from lysosomal degradation.

steps/2.description: Listeriolysin O is a cholesterol-dependent pore-forming cytolysin. It ruptures the phagosomal membrane before the lysosome can fuse with it, and the bacterium reaches the cytosol alive. This is the step that separates Listeria from the bacteria that macrophages simply digest.

evidence.snippet: The actin assembly-inducing protein (ActA) plays a critical role in the intracellular motility of LM. Upon entry into the host–cell cytoplasm, LM hijacks the host’s actin cytoskeleton to facilitate its movement through a mechanism known as actin-based motility. ActA is essential in this process as it catalyzes the polymerization of actin filaments at one pole of the bacterium, generating actin tails that propel the bacterium forward
evidence.explanation: Describes the actin-based motility mechanism this node names.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, LM has evolved a sophisticated mechanism for direct cell-to-cell dissemination, allowing it to transition between host cells without exposure to the extracellular environment, further circumventing immune detection
evidence.explanation: States the immune consequence of spreading cell to cell, which is why this node matters clinically.

steps/3.description: ActA polymerises host actin at one pole of the bacterium. The comet tail drives it through the cytoplasm and into a protrusion, the neighbouring cell engulfs the protrusion, and the organism has moved house without ever entering the extracellular space. Antibody and complement never get a look at it.

evidence.snippet: The adaptive response to Listeria involves Th1-type CD4+ T cells, which produce IFN-γ and activate cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. These cells are critical for recognizing and killing infected host cells. However, the shift toward a Th2-dominant immune profile during pregnancy can reduce the efficiency of Th1 responses, making it more challenging to fight off intracellular pathogens like LM
evidence.explanation: States the Th1 mechanism of control and the pregnancy-associated Th2 shift that weakens it.

steps/4.description: Th1 CD4 cells producing interferon gamma, and the cytotoxic CD8 cells they license, are what kill infected cells. Pregnancy shifts the immune profile towards Th2, and the shift is why pregnancy is a risk factor for an organism that hides inside cells. Age, immunosuppression, malignancy and cirrhosis work on the same limb.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, listerial disease, or listeriosis, most often presents as bacteremia, meningitis or meningoencephalitis, and pregnancy-associated infections manifesting as miscarriage or neonatal sepsis.
evidence.explanation: Names bacteraemia and the two invasive destinations that this node branches to.

steps/5.description: Bacteraemia. From the blood the organism reaches two places that matter more than the rest: the central nervous system and, in pregnancy, the placenta. Both crossings use the same internalin machinery that got it through the gut.

evidence.snippet: The fatality risk factors were the involvement of the central nervous system, hyperbilirubinemia, and hyponatremia for all enrolled subjects.
evidence.explanation: Identifies central nervous system involvement as an independent fatality risk factor by logistic regression, which is why this node is the one that changes prognosis.

steps/6.description: Neurolisteriosis. Meningitis and meningoencephalitis are the usual forms, and brainstem rhombencephalitis is the one that is nearly specific to this organism. In a 71-patient cohort neurolisteriosis carried a higher fatality than bacteraemia alone, and central nervous system involvement was itself an independent fatality risk factor.

evidence.snippet: LM typically transmits from the mother to the fetus through the placenta, with transmission most commonly occurring during the third trimester when the placenta is more susceptible to infection.

evidence.snippet: Another pivotal virulence factor is listeriolysin O (LLO), a pore-forming toxin that facilitates the bacterium’s escape from the phagosome into the host–cell’s cytoplasm following engulfment. evidence.snippet: The actin assembly-inducing protein (ActA) plays a critical role in the intracellular motility of LM. Upon entry into the host–cell cytoplasm, LM hijacks the host’s actin cytoskeleton to facilitate its movement through a mechanism known as actin-based motility. evidence.snippet: The adaptive response to Listeria involves Th1-type CD4+ T cells, which produce IFN-γ and activate cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. However, the shift toward a Th2-dominant immune profile during pregnancy can reduce the efficiency of Th1 responses, making it more challenging to fight off intracellular pathogens like LM

edges/3.description: The intracellular niche is what makes containment depend on T cell immunity rather than on antibody.

evidence.snippet: In the treatment of listeriosis, β-lactam antibiotics are considered the first-line therapy. Ampicillin and amoxicillin are the preferred agents for treating listeriosis during pregnancy. These antibiotics inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking, which is crucial for bacterial viability.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the first-line status and the mechanism of the agents named here.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, several classes of antibiotics, including cephalosporins, clindamycin, and chloramphenicol, are known to be ineffective against LM.
evidence.explanation: Records the negative that matters at the bedside. Cephalosporin-based empirical cover misses this organism.

treatments/0.description: The first-line therapy, at high dose and intravenously for invasive disease. These agents block peptidoglycan cross-linking. The clinically important negative is that cephalosporins do not work against this organism, which is why empirical meningitis regimens add ampicillin whenever Listeria is plausible.

evidence.snippet: In the treatment of listeriosis, β-lactam antibiotics are considered the first-line therapy. Ampicillin and amoxicillin are the preferred agents for treating listeriosis during pregnancy. These antibiotics inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking, which is crucial for bacterial viability.
evidence.explanation: States the drug class, its molecular target and that viability depends on it.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Blocking cell wall synthesis kills replicating organisms and so ends the intracellular expansion this node describes.

evidence.explanation: Names gentamicin alongside ampicillin as the antibiotic treatment for maternal and neonatal disease.

treatments/1.description: An aminoglycoside added to the beta-lactam in severe disease, for synergy. The incremental benefit is not established and it carries nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, so its use is selective.
